                                   PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

                                                     §
    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §             BEFORE THE
  LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                         §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
  STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                     §              OF TEXAS

    TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY’S COMMENTS TO COMMISSION
                 STAFF’S QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Texas-New Mexico Power Company (“TNMP”) respectfully submits these comments to
the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) in response to the Commission Staff’s
January 2, 2026, Second Discussion, related to Rulemaking to Implement Large Load
Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561. TNMP appreciates the opportunity to submit
these comments and looks forward to collaborating with Commission Staff on this project.
                         I.     Response to Commission Staff’s Questions
Questions 3-4:
3. Should the commission maintain the definition for an interconnecting utility that is set forth
in Attachment C? If not, what definition should be used?
4. If the commission maintains the definition for an interconnecting utility that is set forth in
Attachment C, what framework should the rule establish for ensuring that the interconnecting
transmission service provider receives the required security and CIAC in instances where the
certificated retail utility and interconnecting transmission service provider are different entities?


       TNMP agrees with the Commission’s stated definition for an interconnecting utility set
forth in Attachment C.


        “The electric utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is
       certificated to serve the interconnecting large load customer at retail or, if the
       certificated utility designates, the interconnecting transmission service provider.”




                                                 1
           The interconnecting utility must be the utility certificated to serve load in the applicable
service territory, except in limited circumstances with the certificated retail utility affirmatively
designates the interconnecting transmission service provider. A large load interconnection, even
one occurring at transmission voltage, receives transmission service for retail load therefore must
be served by a retail utility. Although some large loads may seek to become wholesale market
participants in the future, they are not market participants today. Until that time, large loads remain
retail loads and must be served by the retail utility certificated for the territory in which the load is
located. Serving retail load through a utility outside of its certificated retail service territory is
inappropriate and unsupported by Commission rules.
          Permitting a utility that does not hold the retail certificate for a territory to interconnect and
charge customers would eliminate any meaningful limits on utility service obligations and
ultimately dismantle certificated service territories in Texas. Such an outcome would replace the
Commission’s longstanding certification territory framework with ad hoc utility selection,
inconsistent with PURA and Commission precedent.
          TNMP opposes any framework that would allow an interconnecting transmission service
provider to receive required security or assess a contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) where
the certificated retail utility and the interconnecting transmission service provider are different
entities and the retail load is served outside the retail utility’s certificated service territory. CIAC
is a tariff-based mechanism and exists solely because a customer is subject to a Commission
approved retail tariff. If a utility does not own the retail service territory and the end use large load
customer is not subject to that utility’s tariff, there is no legal or regulatory basis for that utility to
assess or collect a CIAC. CIAC authority does not exist independently and cannot be implied
outside of a retail tariff relationship.
          Providing only an ESID does not constitute providing retail service. If a load is deemed
not to be a retail customer of the interconnecting utility, then the customer cannot be subject to
that utility’s tariffs. Most critically, where a load is treated as non-retail while receiving
transmission service for retail load from a separate interconnecting transmission service provider
outside the certificated service territory, the customer is not clearly subject to any retail utility’s
tariff.
          This creates a regulatory void in which customers and utilities lack clear tariff protections,
obligations and remedies. This is dangerous for both customers and utilities, and undermines the


                                                      2
 Commission’s longstanding customer protection goals. Without defined retail utility relationships,
customers lack tariff based recourse, utilities lack tariff based protections, and the Commission’s
ability to resolve disputes or enforce obligations becomes convoluted.
       Allowing non-certificated utilities to act as interconnecting utilities for retail large load
interconnections would result in the functional elimination of certificated service territories,
improper assessment of CIAC without tariff authority, and erosion of clear and necessary
regulatory protections for both customers and utilities alike.


Question 13. If the commission adopts a process whereby ERCOT, not the interconnecting
utility, reallocates capacity on a system-wide basis through a batch study process, what
parameters should the commission establish for such a process?
       There is significant uncertainty among utilities and customers regarding how existing
customers with outstanding load requests are to be treated in the batch study proposed framework.
TNMP requests that any Commission-approved batch study or systemwide capacity reallocation
process prioritize pre-existing load requests over new requests.
       Customers that entered the interconnection or service queue years ago, when there was
limited capacity, must not be overlooked by new requests simply because new capacity later
becomes available. Any newly available capacity should first be applied to satisfy previously
submitted and pending load requests, including those that have been waiting for years. New
entrants should not be permitted to capture newly available capacity ahead of pre-existing
customers in the queue. This is a basic fairness principle and essential to preserving confidence in
the interconnection process.
       Accordingly, TNMP requests that the Commission establish chronological priority (first-
in, first-out) as a foundational parameter of the batch study process. Many customers executed
interconnection agreements years ago, contributed significant financial capital, and accepted
Commission approved timelines for service. Those customers relied on the integrity of the existing
processes and should not be disadvantaged by a later systemwide reallocation that ignores queue
position. TNMP requests that the Commission require ERCOT to clearly identify and protect
existing customers with pending requests within the batch study methodology, rather than treating
all requests as if they entered the system at the same time.




                                                 3
        TNMP appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments, reserves its right to comment
further as to other issues, and looks forward to continuing to work with the Commission and Staff
on these important issues.


                                                    Respectfully submitted,

  STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                        §              OF TEXAS

      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY’S
                            COMMENTS

        Texas-New Mexico Power Company (“TNMP”) respectfully submits this executive
summary of its comments to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) in response
to the Commission Staff’s Second Discussion related to large load interconnection standards.
TNMP supports economic growth and industrial development, however these objectives must be
considered with prudent utility investment and coordinated grid planning at the forefront.

        TNMP’s overarching recommendations confirm that modifications to the Commission’s
framework should ensure that large load interconnections are evaluated in a manner focused on
both system reliability and protection of ratepayers, providing for a fair, transparent, and consistent
process across all utilities.

        TNMP highlights the following three recommendations for Commission review:

                a) TNMP supports the Commission’s proposed definition of interconnecting
                    utility in which the interconnecting utility is the retail utility certificated to serve
                    the load.

                b) Retail service must follow existing certificated retail territories. Allowing
                    utilities outside certificated territories to serve retail load is unsupported by
                    Commission rules and inconsistent with PURA.

                c) Permitting non-certificated utilities to interconnect and charge retail customers
                    would erode certificated service utilities and replace longstanding regulatory
                    framework and support ad hoc utility selection.

                d) CIAC is a tariff based mechanism that may only be assessed by the certificated
                    retail utility.


                                                    5
 e) Providing only an ESID does not constitute retail service.

f) Frameworks that separate interconnection from retail service creates regulatory
   gaps depriving utilities of necessary tariff protections and putting customer
   recourse at risk.

g) ERCOT batch study or systemwide capacity reallocation processes must
   prioritize pre-existing load requests over new requests to preserve fairness in
   the interconnection process.

h) The Commission should require chronological priority as a foundational
   parameter to protect customers who executed interconnection agreements,
   invested capital, and accepted extended timelines in reliance on existing
   processes at the time of interconnection.
